newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia progresses on oil laws - US energy head Pena.
newsitem.headline: Russia progresses on oil laws - US energy head Pena.

text.p: U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena said on Wednesday he thought Moscow had made progress in attracting foreign oil investors to Russia.

"We are pleased with the legislation that is going through the Duma (the lower parliament house) and we are hopeful that additional enabling legislation required for the agreements will be passed," he told a news conference.

Pena said he had discussed with Duma deputies which oil and mineral reserves would be open to production-sharing deals, adding that he hoped the next list approved would included certain sites under consideration by U.S. oil companies.

U.S. and other oil companies, which are ready to invest around $60 billion in Russia's oil sector if the right legislation is in place, have complained Moscow has dragged its feet on passing the laws needed for deals to get off the ground.
"The fact is that Russia has vast energy reserves and by many accounts international companies are ready to invest $60 billion in Russia's oil industry," Pena said.
"But those investments are awaiting the development of a stable and transparent legal and regulatory framework to support them."

The projects over their lives would generate $600 billion for the Russian economy and create 500,000 jobs, Pena said, adding, "so it is in everyone's interest to see energy markets develop and open as quickly as possible here in Russia."
Russia has been losing oil investment dollars to its former Soviet neighbours Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan, where major multi-billion dollar projects are proceeding more quickly.

Moscow has passed a production-sharing law, but it is flawed and requires amendments. One sore point with foreign oil executives is that most projects must be approved by the Duma, which is slowly drawing up lists of reserves open to output-sharing deals.
President Boris Yeltsin signed into law on Tuesday the first list, comprising seven mineral and oil reserves. Only one of the oil fields on the list is under consideration by a foreign investor.
Foreign oil companies also want guarantees they will be able to export their share of output through Russia's crowded pipeline system.
Russia is the world's third-largest crude oil producer, but it will need large foreign investment dollars if it is to tap its next generation of reserves.
But some conservative politicians fear Moscow is opening up its strategic energy sector too quickly and too widely.

Pena said he had countered those fears by pointing out to some Duma deputies that British Petroleum is the largest oil producer in the United States, while Shell International is the biggest operator in the Gulf of Mexico.
